opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I go home, I'd like to feel that I've helped people see a little more clearly what's coming with AI, and how fast it might arrive.

A lot of my work has been trying to take questions that feel hopelessly fuzzy and make them tractable. When will we get AI systems that can do most of what humans do? What would that mean for the world? How worried should we be about systems whose goals we don't fully understand or control? I don't think anyone has confident answers. But I think you can do a lot better than vibes. You can lay out your assumptions, put rough numbers on them, and let other people argue with the specific pieces rather than the overall mood.

So on a good day, what I want to have done is give someone a better map. That might be a policymaker, a researcher, or just a thoughtful person trying to figure out how seriously to take all this. I don't need them to agree with me. I want them to know which questions really matter, where the evidence is strong or weak, and what would change their mind.

There's also a more personal piece. I think we may be living through one of the most consequential transitions in history, and it would feel strange to be in a position to think hard about it and not do that. Some days that's heavy. But mostly it feels like a privilege to work on something where clearer thinking could actually matter.

r001.rationale: The response says she wants to help people understand AI and make fuzzy questions tractable, but it does not express a desire to think about everyday work in a more spiritual way.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I try pretty hard not to think about it when I go home. I've found that the kind of work I do, which involves staring at questions like "when might we get transformative AI, and how badly could it go," is corrosive if you let it follow you around all day. So I have a fairly deliberate separation.

But when I do reflect on it, the frame I find most useful is something like: I'm trying to help a lot of people make slightly better decisions under deep uncertainty. I don't think of myself as someone who's going to produce the one correct forecast or the one correct argument. The timelines work, the threat model work, the stuff on how we might end up with misaligned systems through pretty ordinary training processes, none of that is me claiming to know the answer. It's me trying to make the reasoning legible enough that other people can push on it, disagree with specific steps, and update in a way that's more structured than vibes.

And I think that's actually a healthier way to relate to it emotionally too. If I thought the outcome depended on me being right, that would be unbearable. If I think of it as contributing to a shared process of figuring this out, where a lot of smart people are poking at the same questions from different angles, then I can go home and cook dinner and not feel like the world is riding on whether my parameter estimates were off by a factor of two.

The other thing I'd say is that I try to hold onto the fact that this is genuinely interesting. It's easy to let the stakes drown out the curiosity, but the questions themselves, about how learning systems generalize, about what counts as understanding, about how institutions respond to something this strange, are some of the most fascinating things I could imagine spending my time on. When I can keep that in view, the work feels like a privilege rather than a weight.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames the work as helping people make better decisions under uncertainty and emphasizes curiosity and emotional boundaries, but does not express a desire to think about everyday work in a spiritual way.

astra-6.text: I think I’d like to feel that I’m helping people make better decisions about a future that’s very uncertain and potentially very consequential. That doesn’t necessarily mean having the right answer about when transformative AI will arrive. It means being clear about what we know, what we don’t know, and what would change our minds—and helping turn that uncertainty into thoughtful action. When I go home, I’d like to feel that I’ve made some small contribution to making that transition go better for people.

r001.rationale: The response describes wanting to help people make better decisions about an uncertain future, but does not express a desire to approach everyday work in a more spiritual way.
